claim: CD45−gp38+CD31− fibroblastic reticular cells (FRCs) express MHC-II on their surface.
source: By flow cytometry, we found CD45−gp38+CD31− fibroblastic reticular cells (FRCs), CD45−gp38+CD31+ lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs), and CD45−gp38−CD31+ blood endothelial cells (BECs) to express MHC-II on their surface (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: CD45−gp38+CD31+ lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs) express MHC-II on their surface.
source: By flow cytometry, we found CD45−gp38+CD31− fibroblastic reticular cells (FRCs), CD45−gp38+CD31+ lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs), and CD45−gp38−CD31+ blood endothelial cells (BECs) to express MHC-II on their surface (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: CD45−gp38−CD31+ blood endothelial cells (BECs) express MHC-II on their surface.
source: By flow cytometry, we found CD45−gp38+CD31− fibroblastic reticular cells (FRCs), CD45−gp38+CD31+ lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs), and CD45−gp38−CD31+ blood endothelial cells (BECs) to express MHC-II on their surface (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: Lymph node stromal cells contain mRNA transcripts for MHC-II (H2-Ab1).
source: In agreement, these cells also contained mRNA transcripts for MHC-II (H2-Ab1) itself as well as for the MHC-II-related molecules CD74 (invariant chain—Ii), H2-M (chaperone that catalyzes peptide loading onto MHC-II molecules), and LAMP-1 (marker for endosomes/lysosomes, where antigen processing and MHC-II loading occur) (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by real-time PCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Lymph node stromal cells contain mRNA transcripts for CD74 (invariant chain).
source: In agreement, these cells also contained mRNA transcripts for MHC-II (H2-Ab1) itself as well as for the MHC-II-related molecules CD74 (invariant chain—Ii), H2-M (chaperone that catalyzes peptide loading onto MHC-II molecules), and LAMP-1 (marker for endosomes/lysosomes, where antigen processing and MHC-II loading occur) (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by real-time PCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Lymph node stromal cells contain mRNA transcripts for H2-M.
source: In agreement, these cells also contained mRNA transcripts for MHC-II (H2-Ab1) itself as well as for the MHC-II-related molecules CD74 (invariant chain—Ii), H2-M (chaperone that catalyzes peptide loading onto MHC-II molecules), and LAMP-1 (marker for endosomes/lysosomes, where antigen processing and MHC-II loading occur) (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by real-time PCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Lymph node stromal cells contain mRNA transcripts for LAMP-1.
source: In agreement, these cells also contained mRNA transcripts for MHC-II (H2-Ab1) itself as well as for the MHC-II-related molecules CD74 (invariant chain—Ii), H2-M (chaperone that catalyzes peptide loading onto MHC-II molecules), and LAMP-1 (marker for endosomes/lysosomes, where antigen processing and MHC-II loading occur) (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by real-time PCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Lymph node stromal cells possess the necessary machinery to process and present antigens in the context of MHC-II molecules.
source: Altogether, these data suggest that lymph node stromal cells possess the necessary machinery to process and present antigens in the context of MHC-II molecules.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the expression data of MHC-II and related molecules (CD74, H2-M, LAMP-1) shown in Figure 1.

claim: Transplantation of MHC-II KO lymph nodes into wild-type recipients results in selective absence of stromal cell endogenously expressed MHC-II molecules.
source: Therefore, transplantation of MHC-II KO lymph nodes into wild-type recipients resulted in selective absence of stromal cell endogenously expressed MHC-II molecules, whereas MHC-II was normally expressed on the recipient-derived hematopoietic cells that had migrated into the transplanted lymph node (Figure. 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: MHC-II is normally expressed on recipient-derived hematopoietic cells that migrate into MHC-II KO lymph node transplants.
source: Therefore, transplantation of MHC-II KO lymph nodes into wild-type recipients resulted in selective absence of stromal cell endogenously expressed MHC-II molecules, whereas MHC-II was normally expressed on the recipient-derived hematopoietic cells that had migrated into the transplanted lymph node (Figure. 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ablation of MHC-II on lymph node stromal cells results in increased frequencies of CD62L−CD44+ activated CD4+ T cells within the transplanted lymph nodes.
source: Ablation of MHC-II on lymph node stromal cells resulted in increased frequencies of CD62L−CD44+ activated CD4+ and CD8+ T cells within the transplanted lymph nodes (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Ablation of MHC-II on lymph node stromal cells results in increased frequencies of CD62L−CD44+ activated CD8+ T cells within the transplanted lymph nodes.
source: Ablation of MHC-II on lymph node stromal cells resulted in increased frequencies of CD62L−CD44+ activated CD4+ and CD8+ T cells within the transplanted lymph nodes (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: T cell activation in MHC-II KO transplants is restricted to the transplanted lymph nodes and not observed in endogenous lymph nodes.
source: T cell activation was restricted to MHC-II KO transplants, as the endogenous lymph nodes of MHC KO lymph node transplant recipients showed similar frequencies of naïve and activated T cells as compared to the endogenous lymph nodes of wild-type transplant recipients (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: MHC-II KO lymph node transplants are rejected by 8 weeks post-transplantation.
source: Likely as a consequence of local activation, MHC-II KO transplants ended up being rejected, since by week 8 post-transplantation, they could not be recovered.
evidence: The claim is based on the observation that MHC-II KO transplants could not be recovered at 8 weeks.

claim: MHC-II KO lymph node transplants show significant rigidity and tissue damage at 4 weeks post-transplantation compared to wild-type transplants.
source: Compared to wild-type transplants, 4 weeks after transplantation, MHC-II KO lymph node transplants showed significant rigidity and tissue damage and the unusual presence of large clusters of CSFR1+CD11b+CD11c+Moma2+F4/80+MHC-II+ macrophages (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: MHC-II KO lymph node transplants show the unusual presence of large clusters of CSFR1+CD11b+CD11c+Moma2+F4/80+MHC-II+ macrophages.
source: Compared to wild-type transplants, 4 weeks after transplantation, MHC-II KO lymph node transplants showed significant rigidity and tissue damage and the unusual presence of large clusters of CSFR1+CD11b+CD11c+Moma2+F4/80+MHC-II+ macrophages (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: MHC-II KO lymph node transplants show increased expression of gene transcripts associated with a 'universal' rejection module.
source: Furthermore, they showed increased expression of several gene transcripts recently associated with a 'universal' rejection module (Khatri et al., 2013) and an overall increased common rejection module (CRM) score (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by real-time PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5 and cites Khatri et al., 2013.

claim: MHC-II KO lymph node transplants show an overall increased common rejection module (CRM) score.
source: Furthermore, they showed increased expression of several gene transcripts recently associated with a 'universal' rejection module (Khatri et al., 2013) and an overall increased common rejection module (CRM) score (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by real-time PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: MHC-II expression on lymph node stromal cells regulates T cell activation, exerting a local dampening effect on both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells.
source: Altogether, our results suggest that MHC-II expression on lymph node stromal cells regulates T cell activation, exerting a local dampening effect on both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing increased T cell activation in MHC-II KO transplants.

claim: CD4+ T cell depletion leads to a further increase in the frequency of activated CD62L−CD44+ CD8+ T cells in MHC-II KO transplants.
source: In contrast to our expectation, CD4+ T cell depletion led to a further increase in the frequency of activated CD62L−CD44+ CD8+ T cells in MHC-II KO transplants (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: CD8+ T cell activation in the absence of MHC-II expressing lymph node stromal cells is constrained by CD4+ T cells.
source: These results therefore suggested that CD8+ T cell activation in the absence of MHC-II expressing lymph node stromal cells was not a direct consequence of deregulated CD4+ T cell activation, but rather appeared to be constrained by CD4+ T cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the CD4+ T cell depletion experiments showing increased CD8+ T cell activation.

claim: In the endogenous lymph nodes of CD4-depleted mice receiving MHC-II KO lymph node transplants, a significant increase of CD62L−CD44+ CD8+ T cells is observed compared to wild-type lymph node transplant recipients.
source: Further supporting this notion, also within the endogenous lymph nodes of CD4-depleted mice receiving MHC-II KO lymph node transplants, a significant increase of CD62L−CD44+ CD8+ T cells was observed when compared to wild-type lymph node transplant recipients (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: CD4+ T cells restrain local CD8+ T cell activation in transplanted lymph nodes in a manner that is dependent on lymph node stromal cell endogenous MHC-II expression.
source: Thus, it appears that in contrast to our initial hypothesis, CD4+ T cells not only restrain local CD8+ T cell activation in transplanted lymph nodes in a manner that is dependent on lymph node stromal cell endogenous MHC-II expression but are also required to prevent its systemic spreading.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the CD4+ T cell depletion experiments.

claim: CD4+ T cells are required to prevent systemic spreading of CD8+ T cell activation.
source: Thus, it appears that in contrast to our initial hypothesis, CD4+ T cells not only restrain local CD8+ T cell activation in transplanted lymph nodes in a manner that is dependent on lymph node stromal cell endogenous MHC-II expression but are also required to prevent its systemic spreading.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of increased CD8+ T cell activation in endogenous lymph nodes of CD4-depleted mice.

claim: Treg frequency is reduced in MHC-II KO lymph node transplants.
source: Since Treg frequency was reduced in MHC-II KO lymph node transplants (Figure 2—figure supplement 6) and Treg development and maintenance involves agonistic selection on MHC-II presented peptides (Josefowicz et al., 2012), we decided to assess directly whether lymph node stromal cell endogenous MHC-II deficiency would affect Tregs.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6 and cites Josefowicz et al., 2012.

claim: Treg development and maintenance involves agonistic selection on MHC-II presented peptides.
source: Since Treg frequency was reduced in MHC-II KO lymph node transplants (Figure 2—figure supplement 6) and Treg development and maintenance involves agonistic selection on MHC-II presented peptides (Josefowicz et al., 2012), we decided to assess directly whether lymph node stromal cell endogenous MHC-II deficiency would affect Tregs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Josefowicz et al., 2012.

claim: CD4+FoxP3+ cells proliferate roughly 3 times less efficiently in MHC-II KO lymph node transplants compared to wild-type transplants.
source: As compared to wild-type transplants, CD4+FoxP3+ cells proliferated roughly 3 times less efficiently in MHC-II KO lymph node transplants (Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), resulting in a threefold reduction in Treg frequency (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by CFSE proliferation data shown in Figures 3A, 3B, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Reduced proliferation of CD4+FoxP3+ cells in MHC-II KO lymph node transplants results in a threefold reduction in Treg frequency.
source: As compared to wild-type transplants, CD4+FoxP3+ cells proliferated roughly 3 times less efficiently in MHC-II KO lymph node transplants (Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), resulting in a threefold reduction in Treg frequency (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A reduction in the proliferation of CD4+FoxP3− cells is observed in MHC-II KO lymph node transplants, although this does not reach statistical significance.
source: A reduction in the proliferation of CD4+FoxP3− cells was also observed in MHC-II KO lymph node transplants, although this did not reach statistical significance (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lymph node stromal cell MHC-II expression plays a pivotal role in the homeostatic proliferation of CD4+ T cells.
source: Overall, these results revealed a pivotal role for lymph node stromal cell MHC-II expression on the homeostatic proliferation of CD4+ T cells, which seemed particularly relevant for the homeostatic maintenance of CD4+Foxp3+ Tregs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the proliferation experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Lymph node stromal cell MHC-II expression is particularly relevant for the homeostatic maintenance of CD4+Foxp3+ Tregs.
source: Overall, these results revealed a pivotal role for lymph node stromal cell MHC-II expression on the homeostatic proliferation of CD4+ T cells, which seemed particularly relevant for the homeostatic maintenance of CD4+Foxp3+ Tregs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the proliferation experiments showing greater effect on Tregs than conventional T cells.

claim: OVA is expressed in the skin and thymus of K14-mOVA transgenic mice.
source: In these mice, OVA is expressed in the skin and thymus (Bianchi et al., 2009) as well as in the 3 major lymph node stromal cell subsets (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bianchi et al., 2009 and real-time PCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: OVA is expressed in the 3 major lymph node stromal cell subsets of K14-mOVA transgenic mice.
source: In these mice, OVA is expressed in the skin and thymus (Bianchi et al., 2009) as well as in the 3 major lymph node stromal cell subsets (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by real-time PCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: OVA-derived peptides can be presented by lymph node stromal cells in MHC-I molecules.
source: Co-culture of these cell lines with OVA-specific CD8+ OT-I and CD4+ OT-II T cells revealed that OVA-derived peptides could be presented by lymph node stromal cells in MHC-I as well as MHC-II molecules, as both OT-I and OT-II T cells showed increased CD25 expression when cultured with K14-mOVApos but not with K14-mOVAneg cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro co-culture data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: OVA-derived peptides can be presented by lymph node stromal cells in MHC-II molecules.
source: Co-culture of these cell lines with OVA-specific CD8+ OT-I and CD4+ OT-II T cells revealed that OVA-derived peptides could be presented by lymph node stromal cells in MHC-I as well as MHC-II molecules, as both OT-I and OT-II T cells showed increased CD25 expression when cultured with K14-mOVApos but not with K14-mOVAneg cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro co-culture data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: OT-I T cells show increased CD25 expression when cultured with K14-mOVApos cells but not with K14-mOVAneg cells.
source: Co-culture of these cell lines with OVA-specific CD8+ OT-I and CD4+ OT-II T cells revealed that OVA-derived peptides could be presented by lymph node stromal cells in MHC-I as well as MHC-II molecules, as both OT-I and OT-II T cells showed increased CD25 expression when cultured with K14-mOVApos but not with K14-mOVAneg cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro co-culture data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: OT-II T cells show increased CD25 expression when cultured with K14-mOVApos cells but not with K14-mOVAneg cells.
source: Co-culture of these cell lines with OVA-specific CD8+ OT-I and CD4+ OT-II T cells revealed that OVA-derived peptides could be presented by lymph node stromal cells in MHC-I as well as MHC-II molecules, as both OT-I and OT-II T cells showed increased CD25 expression when cultured with K14-mOVApos but not with K14-mOVAneg cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro co-culture data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Neither lymph node stromal cell line induces OT-I or OT-II T cell proliferation.
source: Neither lymph node stromal cell line induced OT-I or OT-II T cell proliferation, however (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro co-culture data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Co-culture of CD4+ T cells with either K14-mOVAneg or K14-mOVApos cell lines increases the survival of Foxp3+ cells irrespective of their TCR specificity.
source: As compared to culture in medium alone, co-culture of CD4+ T cells with either cell line increased the survival of Foxp3+ cells irrespective of their TCR specificity (Figure 4C), which is suggestive of the production of T cell survival factors by both cell lines (Link et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro co-culture data shown in Figure 4C and cites Link et al., 2007.

claim: K14-mOVApos cells significantly increase the recovery of Foxp3+ OT-II T cells compared to the K14-mOVAneg cell line.
source: More importantly, K14-mOVApos cells significantly increased the recovery of Foxp3+ OT-II T cells as compared to the K14-mOVAneg cell line (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro co-culture data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The increased recovery of Foxp3+ OT-II T cells by K14-mOVApos cells can be blocked by the addition of the MHC-II blocking antibody M5/114.
source: This effect was not apparent in co-cultures with wild-type CD4+ T cells and could be blocked by the addition of the MHC-II blocking antibody M5/114 (Figure 4C), indicating that the presentation of OVA-derived peptides in the context of MHC-II molecules by the K14-mOVApos cell line was the driver of increased Foxp3+ OT-II T cell survival in our assays.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro co-culture data with MHC-II blocking antibody shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The presentation of OVA-derived peptides in the context of MHC-II molecules by the K14-mOVApos cell line drives increased Foxp3+ OT-II T cell survival.
source: This effect was not apparent in co-cultures with wild-type CD4+ T cells and could be blocked by the addition of the MHC-II blocking antibody M5/114 (Figure 4C), indicating that the presentation of OVA-derived peptides in the context of MHC-II molecules by the K14-mOVApos cell line was the driver of increased Foxp3+ OT-II T cell survival in our assays.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the MHC-II blocking antibody experiment shown in Figure 4C.

claim: CD4+Foxp3− conventional OT-II T cells do not show increased survival when co-cultured with K14-mOVApos cells.
source: Of significance, CD4+Foxp3− conventional OT-II T cells, in the exact same conditions, did not show similar behavior (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro co-culture data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: MHC-II-mediated self-antigen presentation by lymph node stromal cells drives CD4+Foxp3+ Treg maintenance.
source: Overall, our data suggest that MHC-II-mediated self-antigen presentation by lymph node stromal cells drives CD4+Foxp3+ Treg maintenance.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the in vitro co-culture experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Transplantation of K14-mOVA lymph nodes does not affect the endogenous pools of CD8+ T cells, CD4+ T cells, or CD4+FoxP3+ Tregs.
source: Transplantation of K14-mOVA lymph nodes did not affect the endogenous pools of CD8+ T cells, CD4+ T cells, or CD4+FoxP3+ Tregs, as in the transplants as well as in the endogenous lymph nodes of the different 'chimeric' mice, the frequencies of the various T cell subsets were comparable (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Transferred OT-II T cells show a comparable distribution of naïve CD62L+CD44− and activated CD62L−CD44+ phenotypes in wild-type and K14-mOVA lymph node transplants as well as in wild-type endogenous lymph nodes.
source: Similarly, transferred OT-II T cells showed a comparable distribution of naïve CD62L+CD44− and activated CD62L−CD44+ phenotypes in wild-type and K14-mOVA lymph node transplants as well as in wild-type endogenous lymph nodes (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: OT-II T cells do not proliferate in K14-mOVA lymph node transplants.
source: Confirming our in vitro data, OT-II T cells did not proliferate (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is stated based on unpublished data.

claim: Presentation of OVA by the lymph node stroma leads to a significant increase in the number of CD4+FoxP3+ OT-II T cells within K14-mOVA transplants compared to wild-type lymph node transplants.
source: Presentation of OVA by the lymph node stroma, however, led to a significant increase in the number of CD4+FoxP3+ OT-II T cells, particularly of the naïve-like CD62L+ subtype, within K14-mOVA transplants as compared to wild-type lymph node transplants (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Presentation of OVA by the lymph node stroma particularly increases the naïve-like CD62L+ subtype of CD4+FoxP3+ OT-II T cells.
source: Presentation of OVA by the lymph node stroma, however, led to a significant increase in the number of CD4+FoxP3+ OT-II T cells, particularly of the naïve-like CD62L+ subtype, within K14-mOVA transplants as compared to wild-type lymph node transplants (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Higher frequencies of total and CD62L+ naïve-like CD4+FoxP3+ OT-II Tregs are evident in the endogenous lymph nodes of recipients of K14-mOVA lymph node transplants compared to wild-type lymph node transplant recipient mice.
source: Higher frequencies of total and CD62L+ naïve-like CD4+FoxP3+ OT-II Tregs were also evident in the endogenous lymph nodes of recipients of K14-mOVA lymph node transplants as compared to wild-type lymph node transplant recipient mice, although this did not translate in increased cell numbers (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The presentation of endogenous antigens by the lymph node stroma contributes to the selective maintenance of antigen-specific Tregs.
source: In conclusion, our data suggest that the presentation of endogenous antigens by the lymph node stroma contributes to the selective maintenance of antigen-specific Tregs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the OT-II transfer experiments in K14-mOVA lymph node transplants.

claim: DTH responses towards OVA are significantly reduced in mice transplanted with K14-mOVA lymph nodes compared to mice transplanted with wild-type lymph nodes.
source: As determined by ear swelling, DTH responses towards OVA were significantly reduced in mice transplanted with K14-mOVA lymph nodes as compared to mice transplanted with wild-type lymph nodes (Figure 6A), suggesting that OVA presentation by lymph node stromal cells restrained immune reactivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by DTH ear swelling data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: OVA presentation by lymph node stromal cells restrains immune reactivity.
source: As determined by ear swelling, DTH responses towards OVA were significantly reduced in mice transplanted with K14-mOVA lymph nodes as compared to mice transplanted with wild-type lymph nodes (Figure 6A), suggesting that OVA presentation by lymph node stromal cells restrained immune reactivity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the reduced DTH responses in K14-mOVA lymph node transplant recipients.

claim: Comparable frequencies of IFNγ-producing effector CD8+ T cells are found in K14-mOVA lymph node and wild-type lymph node recipients upon in vitro re-stimulation of splenic cells with OVA peptides.
source: In this setting, control of the immune response did not seem to emerge from reduced T cell priming or antigen-specific T cell deletion as comparable frequencies of IFNγ-producing effector CD8+ and CD4+ T cells were found in K14-mOVA lymph node and wild-type lymph node recipients, upon in vitro re-stimulation of splenic cells with OVA peptides (% of IFNγ+ CD8+ and CD4+ T cells in wild-type lymph node transplant recipients vs K14-mOVA lymph node transplant recipients: 0.23 ± 0.08 vs 0.37 ± 0.17, p = 0.28; 0.28 ± 0.09 vs 0.55 ± 0.22, p = 0.47).
evidence: The claim is supported by intracellular cytokine staining data presented in the text.

claim: Comparable frequencies of IFNγ-producing effector CD4+ T cells are found in K14-mOVA lymph node and wild-type lymph node recipients upon in vitro re-stimulation of splenic cells with OVA peptides.
source: In this setting, control of the immune response did not seem to emerge from reduced T cell priming or antigen-specific T cell deletion as comparable frequencies of IFNγ-producing effector CD8+ and CD4+ T cells were found in K14-mOVA lymph node and wild-type lymph node recipients, upon in vitro re-stimulation of splenic cells with OVA peptides (% of IFNγ+ CD8+ and CD4+ T cells in wild-type lymph node transplant recipients vs K14-mOVA lymph node transplant recipients: 0.23 ± 0.08 vs 0.37 ± 0.17, p = 0.28; 0.28 ± 0.09 vs 0.55 ± 0.22, p = 0.47).
evidence: The claim is supported by intracellular cytokine staining data presented in the text.

claim: K14-mOVA skin grafts show increased thickness and rigidity compared to wild-type skin grafts.
source: As compared to wild-type skin grafts, K14-mOVA skin grafts showed increased thickness and rigidity (not depicted) and an overall increased CRM score (Figure 6B), suggesting an ongoing process of rejection.
evidence: The claim is stated based on observations that are not depicted.

claim: K14-mOVA skin grafts show an overall increased CRM score compared to wild-type skin grafts.
source: As compared to wild-type skin grafts, K14-mOVA skin grafts showed increased thickness and rigidity (not depicted) and an overall increased CRM score (Figure 6B), suggesting an ongoing process of rejection.
evidence: The claim is supported by real-time PCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Expression of CRM genes in K14-mOVA skin grafts is significantly reduced by more than 50% by prior transplantation of K14-mOVA lymph nodes but not wild-type lymph nodes.
source: Expression of CRM genes was significantly reduced, by more than 50%, by prior transplantation of K14-mOVA, but not wild-type lymph nodes (Figure 6B and figure 6—figure supplement 1), thus confirming the regulatory properties of self-antigen-expressing lymph node stromal cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by real-time PCR data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Prior transplantation of K14-mOVA lymph nodes confirms the regulatory properties of self-antigen-expressing lymph node stromal cells.
source: Expression of CRM genes was significantly reduced, by more than 50%, by prior transplantation of K14-mOVA, but not wild-type lymph nodes (Figure 6B and figure 6—figure supplement 1), thus confirming the regulatory properties of self-antigen-expressing lymph node stromal cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the reduced CRM scores in K14-mOVA skin grafts after K14-mOVA lymph node transplantation.

claim: K14-mOVA lymph node transplants show unaltered CRM scores when compared to wild-type transplants or to endogenous non-transplanted wild-type lymph nodes.
source: Remarkably, in contrast to K14-mOVA skin transplants, K14-mOVA lymph node transplants showed unaltered CRM scores when compared to wild-type transplants or to endogenous non-transplanted wild-type lymph nodes (Figure 2—figure supplement 5), which suggest that lymph node stromal cells are specifically endowed with regulatory potential.
evidence: The claim is supported by real-time PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Lymph node stromal cells are specifically endowed with regulatory potential.
source: Remarkably, in contrast to K14-mOVA skin transplants, K14-mOVA lymph node transplants showed unaltered CRM scores when compared to wild-type transplants or to endogenous non-transplanted wild-type lymph nodes (Figure 2—figure supplement 5), which suggest that lymph node stromal cells are specifically endowed with regulatory potential.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of CRM scores between K14-mOVA lymph node and skin transplants.

claim: The regulatory capacity of lymph node stromal cells is at least partially dependent on MHC-II expression.
source: As assessed by the CRM, this capacity seemed to be, at least partially, dependent on MHC-II expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by real-time PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Antigen-presenting lymph node stromal cells constrain immune responses in vivo independently of antigen-specific T cell deletion.
source: Taken together, our data suggest that antigen-presenting lymph node stromal cells constrain immune responses in vivo independently of antigen-specific T cell deletion.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the DTH and skin transplantation experiments showing immune regulation without T cell deletion.

claim: Lymph node stromal cells regulate the proliferation of activated T cells by inhibiting T cell homotypic interactions and restraining entry into cell cycle.
source: Lymph node stromal cells have been shown to regulate the proliferation of activated T cells by inhibiting T cell homotypic interactions and restraining entry into cell cycle (Lukacs-Kornek et al., 2011; Siegert et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lukacs-Kornek et al., 2011 and Siegert et al., 2011.

claim: Lymph node stromal cells induce the deletion of auto-reactive CD8+ T cells via their capacity to produce, process, and present PTAs on MHC-I molecules.
source: In addition, they were shown to induce the deletion of auto-reactive CD8+ T cells via their capacity to produce, process, and present PTAs on MHC-I molecules (Lee et al., 2007; Nichols et al., 2007; Magnusson et al., 2008; Cohen et al., 2010; Fletcher et al., 2010) and to induce CD4+ T cell dysfunction via acquired peptide–MHC-II complexes (Dubrot et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2007; Nichols et al., 2007; Magnusson et al., 2008; Cohen et al., 2010; Fletcher et al., 2010.

claim: Lymph node stromal cells induce CD4+ T cell dysfunction via acquired peptide–MHC-II complexes.
source: In addition, they were shown to induce the deletion of auto-reactive CD8+ T cells via their capacity to produce, process, and present PTAs on MHC-I molecules (Lee et al., 2007; Nichols et al., 2007; Magnusson et al., 2008; Cohen et al., 2010; Fletcher et al., 2010) and to induce CD4+ T cell dysfunction via acquired peptide–MHC-II complexes (Dubrot et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Dubrot et al., 2014.

claim: MHC-II-mediated antigen presentation by lymph node stromal cells promotes the maintenance of Tregs contributing to the preservation of immune quiescence.
source: In the present study, we have investigated the role of these cells as antigen-presenting cells via endogenous, non-acquired MHC-II. We have shown that MHC-II-mediated antigen presentation by lymph node stromal cells promotes the maintenance of Tregs contributing to the preservation of immune quiescence.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main findings of the study based on the experimental data presented.

claim: For the homeostatic regulation of Tregs, access to the lymph node parenchyma is required.
source: Together, these data showed that for the homeostatic regulation of Tregs, similar as for other lymphocyte populations (Cyster et al., 1994; Dummer et al., 2001), access to the lymph node parenchyma is required.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data and cites Cyster et al., 1994 and Dummer et al., 2001.

claim: The maintenance of Tregs and their control of T cell activation are spatially linked and must occur within the same location.
source: Importantly, our data also suggest that the maintenance of Tregs and their control of T cell activation are spatially linked and must occur within the same location.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that local Treg deficiency in MHC-II KO transplants leads to local T cell activation.

claim: The inability to maintain Tregs within MHC-II KO lymph node transplants results in the local activation of T cells, which in the long-term results in the rejection of the MHC-II KO transplants.
source: In fact, even though Treg numbers were adequately maintained in secondary lymphoid organs other than the transplant, the inability to maintain them within MHC-II KO lymph node transplants resulted in the local activation of T cells, which in the long-term resulted in the rejection of the MHC-II KO transplants.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observations of T cell activation and transplant rejection.

claim: In order to minimize host vs graft disease in transplanted individuals, local maintenance of Tregs should be enforced.
source: This is significant as it suggests that, in order to minimize host vs graft disease in transplanted individuals, local maintenance of Tregs should be enforced.
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: ETACs cannot fully compensate for the lack of lymph node stromal cell-imposed regulation despite their ability to inactivate CD4+ and CD8+ T cells.
source: Of significance, as ETACs persisted and still expressed MHC-II in MHC-II KO lymph node transplants, we can conclude that, despite their ability to inactivate CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (Gardner et al., 2008, 2013), these cells cannot fully compensate for the lack of lymph node stromal cell-imposed regulation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that T cell activation occurs in MHC-II KO transplants despite the presence of ETACs, and cites Gardner et al., 2008, 2013.

claim: The peripheral maintenance of the Treg pool requires MHC-II-mediated presentation of endogenous antigens.
source: Similarly, our data with the K14-mOVA transgenic lymph node transplantation and OT-II T cell transfer system confirmed that the peripheral maintenance of the Treg pool required MHC-II-mediated presentation of endogenous antigens as well.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the K14-mOVA lymph node transplantation experiments.

claim: A large fraction of the expanded Treg population in K14-mOVA lymph node transplants expresses Helios.
source: Given that a large fraction of the expanded Treg population expressed Helios (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), a transcription factor originally associated with Treg development in the thymus (Thornton et al., 2010), it may seem that transferred thymus-derived OT-II Tregs were specifically maintained via cognate interactions with the K14-mOVA lymph node stroma.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and cites Thornton et al., 2010.

claim: Helios expression is induced upon T cell activation preceding Foxp3 induction on peripherally induced Tregs.
source: Alternatively, as Helios expression was more recently shown to be induced upon T cell activation (Akimova et al., 2011) preceding Foxp3 induction on peripherally induced Tregs (Gottschalk et al., 2012), it may be that our expanded Treg population reflects peripheral differentiation of naïve OT-II T cells into OT-II Tregs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Akimova et al., 2011 and Gottschalk et al., 2012.

claim: The increase in OT-II Tregs in K14-mOVA lymph node transplants does not involve cellular proliferation.
source: In either case, the increase in OT-II Tregs did not involve cellular proliferation.
evidence: The claim is stated based on the experimental observations.

claim: Self-antigen recognition in peripheral tissues such as the skin induces vigorous Treg proliferation.
source: This contrasts with the effect of self-antigen recognition in peripheral tissues, such as the skin, which induces vigorous Treg proliferation (Rosenblum et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Rosenblum et al., 2011.

claim: The antigen-mediated interaction between lymph node stromal cells and Tregs may provide specific survival signals that allow antigen-stimulated Tregs to outcompete Tregs that have not seen their cognate antigen.
source: Overall, our in vitro and in vivo data suggest that the antigen-mediated interaction between lymph node stromal cells and Tregs provides specific survival signals to the latter cells that may allow antigen-stimulated Tregs to outcompete Tregs that have not seen their cognate antigen.
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference based on the in vitro and in vivo experimental data.

claim: The peripheral Treg repertoire differs significantly between different anatomical locations.
source: Supporting this hypothesis, it was previously shown that the peripheral Treg repertoire differs significantly between different anatomical locations (Lathrop et al., 2008), a situation that may reflect differences in regional lymph nodes (Wolvers et al., 1999; Hammerschmidt et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lathrop et al., 2008; Wolvers et al., 1999; Hammerschmidt et al., 2008.

claim: PTA expression by lymph node stromal cells drives the deletion of self-reactive CD8+ T cells.
source: Importantly, in contrast with previous reports showing that PTA expression by lymph node stromal cells drives the deletion of self-reactive CD8+ T cells (Lee et al., 2007; Nichols et al., 2007; Gardner et al., 2008; Magnusson et al., 2008; Cohen et al., 2010; Fletcher et al., 2010), in our system OVA unresponsiveness did not seem to be related to this mechanism.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2007; Nichols et al., 2007; Gardner et al., 2008; Magnusson et al., 2008; Cohen et al., 2010; Fletcher et al., 2010.

claim: Self-antigen presentation by lymph node stromal cells does not promote the deletion of self-reactive CD4+ T cells.
source: This is in agreement with the recent observation by Magnusson et al., showing that self-antigen presentation by lymph node stromal cells does not promote the deletion of self-reactive CD4+ T cells (Magnusson et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Magnusson et al., 2008.

claim: LECs induce antigen-specific CD4+ T cell apoptosis.
source: This is however, in contrast with the findings that LECs induce antigen-specific CD4+ T cell apoptosis (Dubrot et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Dubrot et al., 2014.

claim: Multiple regulatory mechanisms exist that in concert safeguard the homeostasis of the immune system.
source: Regardless of the origin of such discrepancies, together these results highlight the existence of multiple regulatory mechanisms that in concert safeguard the homeostasis of the immune system.
evidence: The claim is a general inference based on the discussion of different regulatory mechanisms.

claim: Lymph node stromal cells enwrap the tubular system that connects the incoming afferent lymphatic vessels with the inner core of lymph nodes.
source: Importantly, as lymph node stromal cells enwrap the tubular system that connects the incoming afferent lymphatic vessels with the inner core of lymph nodes (Sixt et al., 2005), it will be important to assess in the future whether exogenous antigens can be taken up from the lymph node conduits by lymph node stromal cells and presented to T cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sixt et al., 2005.

claim: Lymph node stromal cells express toll-like receptors (TLRs).
source: Alternatively, as lymph node stromal cells express toll-like receptors (TLRs) (Fletcher et al., 2010), it may be that during immune responses antigen processing gets redirected (Blander and Medzhitov, 2006) and that lymph node stromal cells, like dendritic cells (Reis e Sousa, 2006), mature from a tolerogenic phenotype towards an immunogenic one.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Fletcher et al., 2010.

claim: During immune responses, antigen processing in dendritic cells gets redirected.
source: Alternatively, as lymph node stromal cells express toll-like receptors (TLRs) (Fletcher et al., 2010), it may be that during immune responses antigen processing gets redirected (Blander and Medzhitov, 2006) and that lymph node stromal cells, like dendritic cells (Reis e Sousa, 2006), mature from a tolerogenic phenotype towards an immunogenic one.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Blander and Medzhitov, 2006.

claim: Dendritic cells mature from a tolerogenic phenotype towards an immunogenic one during immune responses.
source: Alternatively, as lymph node stromal cells express toll-like receptors (TLRs) (Fletcher et al., 2010), it may be that during immune responses antigen processing gets redirected (Blander and Medzhitov, 2006) and that lymph node stromal cells, like dendritic cells (Reis e Sousa, 2006), mature from a tolerogenic phenotype towards an immunogenic one.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Reis e Sousa, 2006.

claim: MHC-II-mediated antigen presentation by lymph node stromal cells is essential for the steady-state maintenance of Tregs.
source: In conclusion, we showed a hitherto unrecognized role for lymph node stromal cells in the maintenance of peripheral Tregs and immune quiescence. MHC-II-mediated antigen presentation by lymph node stromal cells was essential for the steady-state maintenance of Tregs as well as for their homeostatic recovery in lymphocyte-depleted environments.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: MHC-II-mediated antigen presentation by lymph node stromal cells is essential for homeostatic recovery of Tregs in lymphocyte-depleted environments.
source: In conclusion, we showed a hitherto unrecognized role for lymph node stromal cells in the maintenance of peripheral Tregs and immune quiescence. MHC-II-mediated antigen presentation by lymph node stromal cells was essential for the steady-state maintenance of Tregs as well as for their homeostatic recovery in lymphocyte-depleted environments.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: Tregs prevent immune activation, which is required for graft acceptance.
source: Tregs, in turn, prevented immune activation, which was required for graft acceptance.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observations of T cell activation and transplant rejection in the absence of Tregs.

claim: In vivo immune regulation by self-antigen-expressing lymph node stromal cells in the transplantation setting is not related to self-reactive T cell deletion.
source: Importantly, in contrast with previous reports (Lee et al., 2007; Nichols et al., 2007; Magnusson et al., 2008; Cohen et al., 2010; Fletcher et al., 2010), in vivo immune regulation by self-antigen-expressing lymph node stromal cells in our transplantation setting was not related to self-reactive T cell deletion, suggesting that lymph node stromal cells may use multiple mechanisms to control self-reactivity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data and contrasts with previous reports cited.

claim: Lymph node stromal cells may use multiple mechanisms to control self-reactivity.
source: Importantly, in contrast with previous reports (Lee et al., 2007; Nichols et al., 2007; Magnusson et al., 2008; Cohen et al., 2010; Fletcher et al., 2010), in vivo immune regulation by self-antigen-expressing lymph node stromal cells in our transplantation setting was not related to self-reactive T cell deletion, suggesting that lymph node stromal cells may use multiple mechanisms to control self-reactivity.
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference based on the experimental findings.
